classification.tone: Breezy, profane, sexually charged, and increasingly suspenseful with a satirical Hollywood edge

evaluation.positioning_hook: A broke, pretty-boy actor becomes the prime suspect in a serial-killer case after every woman he dates turns up dead, forcing him to solve the murders before Hollywood and the cops bury him.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and easy to sell: a handsome aspiring actor, a serial killer, and a public-facing dating trail that turns into a murder trail. The Hollywood setting, dating-app-era social media, and darkly comic dialogue broaden the hook, though the adult tone and niche industry satire keep it from feeling four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: Jericho dates women, those women die, and the police start circling him while he tries to identify the real killer. The script keeps the engine simple and readable, with the social-media check-ins and the repeated pattern of dates-to-deaths making the premise easy to track.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jericho has a strong surface engine — vain, charming, horny, and suddenly cornered — and Ben gives him a workable comic counterweight. The supporting women are vivid in entrance and function well as pressure points, but the character web is built more around the premise than around deep personal turns.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldness comes from its tonal mashup of serial-killer suspense, actor-world satire, and shameless romantic-comedy behavior. The repeated use of casting rooms, agents, Twitch, comedy clubs, and social media as story machinery gives it a specific angle rather than a generic murder mystery.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps moving through a clean chain of dates, murders, police suspicion, and Jericho’s increasingly reckless attempts to clear himself. The middle section has enough reversals and comic propulsion to keep pages turning, and the interrogation/jail stretch gives the plot a strong pressure spike.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh in a way that clicks immediately: a handsome aspiring leading man whose dating life becomes the evidence trail in a serial-killer case. The combination of vanity, public image, and murder investigation creates a premise that is both novel and instantly understandable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Hollywood-adjacent world is specific and story-generating, with auditions, agents, screen tests, streamers, comics, and low-rent apartments all feeding the plot. The script uses that ecosystem well, though the world functions primarily as a pressure cooker for the central premise rather than as a fully layered institutional maze.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is sharply defined: raunchy, self-aware, and lightly absurd, but anchored by real murder stakes and police suspicion. The dialogue rhythm, sexual frankness, and industry jokes create a voice that would be recognizable within a few pages.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script is strongest as a propulsive, high-concept ride, with the deeper thematic material mostly sitting in the background: image, objectification, and the way public persona can become evidence. There are seeds for more emotional or psychological layering, but the draft mostly chooses momentum and joke density over hidden reserves.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jericho and Ben have the clearest recurring dynamic, and the police duo adds a second useful engine. The women around Jericho create strong scene-to-scene friction, but most relationships serve the central plot rather than generating fully independent story energy.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a charismatic, conventionally handsome male actor
Several roles depend on strong comic timing

notable_requirements: Ranch home / town home / row home variations

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic screen inserts, social media interfaces, and crime-scene visuals.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood effects, stabbing effects, body aftermaths, and a car-vs-pedestrian impact beat.

rights_flags.detail: Classic rock is referenced in the Charger scenes, but no specific song title is plot-critical.
DoorDash, Twitch, Facebook, TMZ, CAA, SAG, and social platforms are named prominently.
Big Moon Entertainment is a fictional company name used as a production entity inside the story.
Waiting for Godot / Gal Gadot riff, Romeo and Juliet, and other public-domain or title-adjacent references are used as dialogue material.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature or mid-budget theatrical genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: festival-to-platform, streamer original, or limited theatrical for adult genre audiences

cost.note: Contemporary, mostly contained locations, practical effects, and no VFX-heavy set pieces keep this in a modest feature budget lane.

cast.note: The lead benefits from a recognizable, very castable handsome male actor, and several attractive 20s female roles plus police and industry parts need strong comic performers.

location.note: The story moves through a dozen-plus contemporary locations across Los Angeles, but they are all accessible real-world spaces rather than built environments.

content.note: Serial murder, sexual dialogue, profanity, and repeated stabbing deaths push the material firmly into mature territory.

rights.note: The script leans on named platforms, entertainment-industry references, and title-adjacent public-domain riffs that should be cleared or lightly adjusted.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives a buyer a clean, high-concept hook that can be sold in one sentence and understood by a broad genre audience. It’s the kind of setup that can attract streamer interest because the premise itself does a lot of the marketing work.
strengths.evidence: Jericho dates women, those women are murdered, and the police begin treating him like the common thread.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jericho is a built-in movie-star role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead combines vanity, charm, sexual confidence, and panic in a way that gives an actor a showcase for comedy and suspense at the same time. That makes the project attractive to reps looking for a role that can reframe a client as a leading man.
strengths.evidence: Jericho’s audition, his agent’s hype, his DoorDash hustle, and his escalating self-importance all sit in the same character lane.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Hollywood satire is baked into the engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The script isn’t just set in entertainment; it uses auditions, agents, screen tests, streamers, and career desperation as part of the murder mystery’s pressure system. That makes it especially attractive to buyers who want a genre piece with insider texture and a built-in conversation starter.
strengths.evidence: Big Moon auditions, Logan’s office, Valerie’s Twitch fame, and the repeated talk of credits, SAG, and screen tests.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone has a sharp comic voice.
strengths.what_it_means: The dialogue is fast, profane, and self-aware, which gives the material a clear identity in a crowded genre field. That voice is a magnet for directors and actors who want a script that can play laughs without losing the murder-story tension.
strengths.evidence: The banter between Jericho and Ben, the interrogation-room insults, and the comedy-club sequences all carry the same rhythm.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The police storyline adds real procedural pressure.
strengths.what_it_means: Alan and Denise give the movie a second engine beyond Jericho’s panic, which helps the script feel like a true thriller rather than just a dating-gone-wrong comedy. That dual-track structure broadens the appeal to buyers who want both character comedy and crime momentum.
strengths.evidence: The whiteboard casework, surveillance, interrogation, warrant search, and eventual arrest all create a parallel investigation track.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The supporting women are vivid and playable.
strengths.what_it_means: Each woman Jericho dates arrives with a distinct comic or social identity — dancer, writer, comic, streamer, ex — which gives casting a lot of color and gives the film a lively dating-world texture. That makes the project attractive to ensemble-minded actors and directors who like scene-stealing supporting turns.
strengths.evidence: Cinnamon, Nikki, Courtney, Valerie, Zoe, and Erika all have distinct entrances and social worlds.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, commercial genre package with a sharp hook: a handsome aspiring actor becomes the suspect in a serial-killer case built out of his own dating life. The script’s real selling point is that it turns Hollywood vanity, social-media exposure, and romantic chaos into a murder mystery with a very specific comic voice.

lead_characters.name: Jericho Hardcastle
lead_characters.hook: Jericho is a hungry, self-mythologizing aspiring actor who knows he’s attractive, knows he’s close to a break, and keeps talking like the world is about to catch up to him. He’s vain without being empty, funny without trying too hard, and reckless enough that his charm keeps turning into evidence against him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Glen Powell in Hit Man or Ryan Gosling in The Nice Guys — a handsome lead whose charisma is the joke, the weapon, and the vulnerability all at once. Actors will chase it for the chance to play vanity, panic, and comic self-delusion while still carrying a thriller.

lead_characters.name: Ben Sanchez
lead_characters.hook: Ben is Jericho’s roommate and creative conscience, a writer who sees the absurdity before anyone else and still keeps feeding the machine. He’s the grounded smart-ass in the room, but he’s also a guy with his own ambition, his own insecurity, and enough loyalty to get dragged into the worst idea in the apartment.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the best-friend engine territory of Jonah Hill in Superbad or Michael Cera in The Disaster Artist — a comic sidekick who gets real scene ownership through timing, frustration, and loyalty. Character actors and comic leads who want a role with sharp banter and emotional utility will want this.

lead_characters.name: Detective Alan James
lead_characters.demographics: Male · mid 50s · tall, thin, receding hairline
lead_characters.hook: Alan is the old-school homicide detective who trusts his gut, hates being slowed down, and is convinced the handsome actor is hiding something. He brings the hard-edged, slightly abrasive authority that keeps the movie from floating away into pure comedy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Bryan Cranston in Drive — a blunt-force authority figure whose certainty is part of the performance pleasure. Veteran character actors who can play menace, impatience, and procedural obsession will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Detective Denise Slater
lead_characters.demographics: Female · mid 30s · short, curvy, thick glasses
lead_characters.hook: Denise is the rookie who is smarter than her title and more emotionally calibrated than her partner, even when she’s forced to play the junior role. She’s observant, skeptical, and increasingly the one who sees the case with the most clarity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, sharp-edged law-enforcement role that gave Regina King in Seven Seconds or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers room to be both competent and emotionally alive. Actors who want a procedural role with wit, authority, and a slow-burn ascent will want this.

lead_characters.name: Nikki Patel
lead_characters.demographics: Female · mid 20s · short, rail thin, screenwriter
lead_characters.hook: Nikki is a writer with a dry, skeptical edge who immediately clocks Jericho’s vanity and still lets the attraction spark. She’s smart, contemporary, and specific enough that her death lands as more than just another body in the pattern.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp, scene-setting supporting part that gave Zoey Deutch in Set It Up or Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart a chance to make a fast impression in a few scenes. Young actresses who want a memorable, witty role with instant chemistry will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Greta 'Cinnamon' Tippet
lead_characters.demographics: Female · mid 20s · tall, busty redhead, exotic dancer
lead_characters.hook: Cinnamon is all heat, glamour, and self-aware excess, a woman who knows exactly how she reads and weaponizes it. She’s funny, sexual, and vivid enough to feel like a whole movie in a few scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of high-visibility supporting turn that gave Jennifer Coolidge in Promising Young Woman or Kathryn Hahn in Bad Moms room to own the screen with attitude and specificity. Actors who like bold, sexy, comic material will want the chance to make a splash fast.

lead_characters.name: Courtney Willis
lead_characters.hook: Courtney is a working comic with a sharp stage persona and a practical view of the grind, which makes her feel like a real person inside the Hollywood chaos. She’s funny, direct, and one of the few characters who can meet Jericho’s energy without shrinking from it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Tiffany Haddish in Girls Trip or Ayo Edebiri in The Bear — a performer with stage presence, timing, and the ability to make a room lean in. Comedic actresses who want a role that can play both stand-up confidence and real-world vulnerability will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Valerie Jane
lead_characters.hook: Valerie is internet-famous, commercially savvy, and self-aware about the shelf life of attention, which makes her feel like the most modern person in the movie. She’s flirty, strategic, and smart enough to understand how image can be monetized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contemporary, media-literate role that gave Haley Lu Richardson in The Edge of Seventeen or Barbie Ferreira in Euphoria a chance to feel current and specific. Young actresses with a strong social-media footprint or a sharp comic presence will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Zoe Walsh
lead_characters.hook: Zoe is Jericho’s ex, and she carries the resentment, ambition, and bruised pride that make the final stretch of the story snap into place. She’s not just jealous; she’s a person whose career and relationship have both been tangled up in Jericho’s orbit.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of volatile ex-role that gave Riley Keough in The Girlfriend Experience or Jena Malone in Donnie Darko room to turn hurt into menace. Actors who like emotionally charged, late-story reveal material will want the part.

lead_characters.name: Taylor Werner
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 20s · tall, handsome, low-level producer
lead_characters.hook: Taylor is the polished, quietly possessive ex who looks like he belongs in the same industry Jericho is trying to enter. He’s controlled on the surface, but the knife on his wall and the tension in his scenes give him a loaded stillness.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained, suspicious supporting role that gave Patrick Wilson in Little Children or Jake Lacy in A Friend of the Family a chance to play charm with an edge. Actors who can project calm while hiding volatility will want it.

lead_characters.name: Logan Smith
lead_characters.hook: Logan is the polished, transactional agent who treats Jericho like a product and a future payday at the same time. He’s funny, ruthless, and exactly the kind of industry operator who makes the Hollywood satire feel lived-in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of fast-talking industry role that gave Bryan Batt in Mad Men or Rob Corddry in Ballers room to be both comic and predatory. Character actors who can sell charm, pressure, and opportunism will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Yancy Rogers
lead_characters.hook: Yancy is the boss who keeps the detectives in line and reminds the movie that procedure has consequences. He’s brief, but he gives the police side a believable chain of command and a little institutional bite.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority role that gives actors like Lance Reddick in Bosch or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire a chance to make a hard-edged impression quickly. Veteran character actors who can do command in a few lines will want it.

lead_characters.name: Annie
lead_characters.hook: Annie is the roommate who exists to carry the shock of Erika’s death into the domestic world, giving the story a human aftershock. She’s brief but functional, and she helps the murders feel like they land in real lives, not just on a case board.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small but emotionally legible part that gives a young actor a clean scene and a real reaction beat. Emerging performers looking for a crisp, grounded credit would take it.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a sexy, funny thriller without sanding off the danger.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Mid-career indie directors or first-time feature directors with a strong short-form reel in dark comedy, crime, or relationship-driven genre material. The right fit is someone who likes performance-forward scenes, can stage tension in ordinary spaces, and understands how to keep a joke alive inside a murder plot.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards clean blocking, sharp dialogue rhythm, and a confident handle on tonal pivots from flirtation to dread. It’s especially attractive to directors who want to prove they can make a commercial genre movie feel specific without needing spectacle.

buyer_appeal.lane: Streaming genre lane with theatrical-capable packaging
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be greenlit off a charismatic lead, a strong director, and a contained production footprint; there’s no VFX dependency and the set pieces are practical. The serial-killer hook, Hollywood satire, and contemporary social-media angle fit the current adult-genre buy zone for streamers and limited theatrical buyers.

considerations.area: The police engine can carry more independent weight.
considerations.detail: Alan and Denise already give the movie a second track, and the version of the script where their investigation scenes feel slightly more self-propelling would deepen the procedural pleasure without changing the premise. One lever would be to let one of their case-board turns land as a mini-reveal before Jericho catches up, so the audience feels the cops moving in real time.

considerations.area: Jericho’s emotional turn could arrive a beat earlier.
considerations.detail: The script already gives him panic, vanity, and comic denial; a next pass could foreground the moment where the murders stop being a dating problem and become a genuine survival problem. That would make his decision to investigate feel even more inevitable and would sharpen the thriller charge in the middle stretch.

considerations.area: The dating-world pattern is the cleanest simplification lever.
considerations.detail: The story moves through several women, several locations, and several industry-adjacent subcultures, which is part of the fun, but the version where one or two of those encounters are combined could protect momentum and trim setup. Because the premise is already clear, collapsing a couple of beats would keep the escalation front-loaded.

considerations.area: The social-media trail is doing real story work.
considerations.detail: Jericho’s check-ins, profile searches, and public posts are a strong contemporary device, and a future pass could keep that thread even more visible as the case tightens. That would strengthen the modernity of the premise and make the investigation feel even more of-the-moment.

considerations.area: The final reveal has room for a cleaner emotional snap.
considerations.detail: The Zoe/Taylor turn gives the ending a workable culprit and motive chain, and the version where Jericho’s realization lands a touch earlier could let the confrontation breathe before the gunfire. That would give the climax a little more inevitability and make the last stretch hit harder.
